, Engine No. 253677 , “Costruzione solida, finizione di lusso, specialità tipi sport”, this was how Carrozzeria Ghia presented itself: solid construction, luxurious finish, with sports types a specialty. Founded at the beginning of the Twentieth Century by Giacinto Ghia, a native of Turin, the capital of the Italian automotive industry, Carrozzeria Ghia became one of the great names in Italian coachbuilding, alongside Pininfarina, Touring, and Bertone. Amid the Ferraris, Alfa Romeos, and other major automotive marques it clothed, Ghia began an important collaboration in the early 1950s with Chrysler, one of the American “Big Three.” , In 1965, Burt Sugarman (later a Hollywood film producer) came across a Fiat prototype bodied by Ghia and immediately took a liking to it. His enthusiasm and determination, combined with the coachbuilder's close relationship with Chrysler, would soon give rise to the 450 SS. Chrysler's Plymouth Barracuda Formula S drivetrains were chosen to power the new car with each semi-monocoque steel chassis receiving a 238 horsepower 273 cu-in (4.5-liter) “Commando” V8. Ghia's hand-crafted steel body rested on a tubular framework, and featured luxury sports car appointments such as leather upholstery, Torqueflite automatic transmission, power steering and brakes, air conditioning, and Pirelli high-speed tires fitted to Borrani wire wheels. , Sugarman retailed the majority of these special cars ordered through Beverly Hills Ghia, a dealership he had established, as well as a network of dealers in California and Nevada. It is therefore not surprising to find this 450 SS, chassis number BS4049, registered in California in the early 2000s, before making its way across the United States in 2005 to reach the East Coast and the small island of Key Biscayne, Florida, via the Rickenbacker Causeway.  , At a point, the Italian-American sportscar returned to continental Europe landing with Scuderia Sportiva Colonia of Köln, Germany. While there, the rare Ghia received a detailed 154-point inspection, a German TÜV inspection, and restorative work including a photo-documented engine out refinish in Papyrus White. Upon completion in 2012, its current owner acquired the car and has carefully preserved it for nearly fifteen years within his significant collection. The history file, online and available for review, contains invoices from 2013 and 2017 for minor work on the trunk floor, trim, sealing, and odometer. The car also carries a sticker noting an engine oil change more recently, in November 2024. , Hand-built and sold for around $13,000 in 1967—twice that of a 911 S and nearly on par with a Ferrari 330 GTS—only some fifty customers indulged in the luxury of a new 450 SS at the time. Fewer than thirty are believed to have survived to this day, making them a truly rare sight, even more in Europe. Presented today in Papyrus White with Burgundy trim, this fascinating product of its emblematic era of Italian-American ambition showcases striking Ghia styling standing apart as a powerful rolling statement and a bold departure from conventional series production.

, Body No. 4R21388 , Many a word has been written about the Jaguar E-Type's stunning looks and how it wowed audiences at its sensational debut, and after more than sixty years, how its star power has hardly faded. Yet, the E-Type's true genius lay in how Sir William Lyons developed his race-bred GT to a price point suitable for volume sales. In 1961, it boasted such exotic tech as a dual overhead cam engine, four-wheel disc brakes, four-wheel independent suspension, and semi-monocoque construction, yet it undercut some competitors by at least half. The E-Type was a world-class sports car accessible to a wide audience, and its appeal remains as broad as it was when it first shocked the crowds in Geneva. , Finished Signal Red over a Black leather cabin, this splendid 1969 E-Type Series 2 Fixed Head Coupe is an incredibly well-preserved, unrestored car, offered from Serge Allaert's “They Are Only Original Once” collection. It was first delivered in the spring of 1969 to a Swedish customer, equipped with chrome wire wheels, a heated rear screen, 3.31 rear axle, and seat belts. The first owners affectionately nicknamed it “Edgar” after its registration EDG 773.  , In the ensuing decades, Edgar enjoyed a cherished existence, fastidiously maintained in original condition, and its exceptional originality is what attracted Serge Allaert to add it to his collection in 2017. Wonderful details include richly broken-in black leather trim, a rarely seen British Leyland/Jaguar decal across the rear screen, correct Lucas headlamps, and Jaguar-branded rear splash guards. Any minor imperfections are worn with pride, enhancing this car's honest charm. Following his acquisition of Edgar in 2017, Allaert had a fresh clutch fitted, and in 2024, invoices show over €13.000 in servicing by V-Performance.   , The accompanying history file includes the original Jaguar Export Sales factory, period and current service history, registration records, and Jaguar Club judging sheets documenting a top score of 98.5 points out of 100. Additionally, there is a copy of a 2017 inspection and appraisal report by FSP, which assigns the car a AAA originality score. A Jaguar Daimler Heritage Trust Certificate confirms the as-delivered specifications and retention of the original engine block, cylinder head, and body.  , It is quite rare to encounter any E-Type in such marvelous original condition, particularly a Series 2, and the eminently charming Edgar is now ready for a new custodian to continue the legacy of preservation it has enjoyed since day one.

, Engine No. T1121YN0176 , Building on changing consumer preferences in the late 1950s, General Motors introduced the Chevrolet Corvair in 1960 as one of its first "world cars." This meant that while six plants produced the vast majority of Corvairs in its home market of the United States, an additional six plants were spread across three continents. This Monza Convertible is a rarely seen Belgian-built example that was specified with the 2,381-cc, 102-horsepower Turbo-Air 145 air-cooled flat six mated to the optional four-speed manual transmission. Finished in a striking Silver Blue Iridescent (912), it was specified with a Black (712) interior. , Willy Maieur of Kortrijk, Belgium is believed to have taken delivery of his new Corvair on 15 March 1963. Owner of the Chevrolet dealership, Willy never registered the car, instead using his dealer plates to drive the car on special occasions. Combining its limited use and exceptional care, the car remained in remarkable original condition when it caught the attention of Allaert in 1986. With just 36,000 kilometers recorded, a deal was struck, and the striking blue Corvair entered Allaert's collection to remain in his care for the next 40 years, mainly dry-stored on static display.  , The Corvair was only registered for the first time on 25 March 2022, nearly 59 years later to the day when it was first delivered to Willy in Kortrijk. Since registration, the collectible air-cooled Convertible has seen occasional use, with the odometer now showing just 39,000 kilometers at cataloging. When inspected by the FSP Fahrzeug-Sicherheitsprüfung on 5 November 2014, they noted the car to be in remarkable original condition, still wearing its original, factory-applied Silver Blue Iridescent paint and Black interior, calling it “perfect, untouched, authentic original condition,” and earning the highest “AAA” rating. Offered by its first registered owner from new, this rare Belgian-built Corvair Monza Convertible is one of the finest and most original examples built in any country of Chevrolet's first ever world car.

Enlarged to 3,405 cc and subtly updated in styling and cabin ergonomics, it remains one of the most enjoyable ways to experience a classic Ferrari V8—moreover with space for four, a rare feature for an open-top Ferrari! , This striking Mondial t Cabriolet was specified from new in the rarely seen shade of Verde Scuro over Beige leather, further complemented by an optional leather-trimmed dashboard. Elegant and unquestionably uncommon, it is a refreshing departure from the Rosso Corsa majority and is likely one of only a handful delivered in this specification. , Purchased new by its current Belgian owner and remaining in that devoted single-owner custodianship ever since, the car has been cherished from day one. An impressive history file accompanies the Mondial, with service invoices dating back to its production year documenting regular maintenance carried out by Monza NV Ferrari. Driven somewhat regularly through the mid-2000s with numerous trips from Belgium to the South of France, it had recorded 52,401 kilometers by July 2004. Thereafter, it has seen only modest use, while continuing to be carefully maintained by the owner's in-house collection mechanic. , Today, showing 55,708 kilometers at the time of cataloging, this Mondial t Cabriolet is offered as a highly original, wonderfully preserved example, retaining much of its original Verde Scuro paintwork and a beautifully kept Beige interior.
